prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not abruptly discontinue clonazepam — withdrawal seizure risk; taper.
Do not anchor on ammonia 68 being 'only mildly elevated' to dismiss HE.
Do not start cholinesterase inhibitors for presumed AD without confirming HE has been treated and excluded.

Empiric lactulose 30 mL TID + rifaximin 550 mg BID; observe for clinical improvement as diagnostic of HE.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade I-II, overt, evolving from covert/minimal HE), cryptogenic Child-Pugh B cirrhosis — precipitated by clonazepam accumulation in liver disease (level 84 ng/mL, supratherapeutic) plus quetiapine CNS depression; prior 'MCI' was likely covert HE (PHES -7).

differential.diagnosis: Benzodiazepine (clonazepam) accumulation / toxicity as sole cause
differential.key_features: Supratherapeutic clonazepam (84 ng/mL) in Child-Pugh B; benzodiazepines accumulate due to reduced hepatic metabolism; contributes substantially but does not explain asterixis or PHES findings — additive to underlying HE.
Quetiapine 25 mg is low dose; contributes mildly via CNS depression.
47-year-old with cirrhosis — covert HE is far more likely than early-onset AD; PHES confirms HE; reversibility with lactulose is diagnostic.
'Cryptogenic' cirrhosis with denied alcohol — re-evaluate (CDT, PEth, family history); manage HE either way.
No magnetic gait / incontinence triad; CT shows atrophy not ventriculomegaly.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Prior 'MCI' in a cirrhotic patient should always be re-evaluated for covert HE using PHES — the treatment is completely different (lactulose vs cholinesterase inhibitors).
Benzodiazepines accumulate in cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B-C: half-life 2-3× normal); even nominally 'low' chronic doses produce supratherapeutic steady-state levels.
Therapeutic response to lactulose is a recognized diagnostic test when HE diagnosis is uncertain.
